newsitem.title: BRAZIL: ING sees Brazil risk rising through 1998.
newsitem.headline: ING sees Brazil risk rising through 1998.

text.p: Brazil's bloated public sector, slow pace of reforms and overvalued currency are likely to raise the risk faced by equities and fixed-income investors here through 1998, a top ING Barings economist said.

"We are likely to witness an increase in country risk from now on, and especially next year," Arturo Porzecanski, ING managing director and chief economist for the Americas, wrote in a report released this week.
"This suggests that Brazilian bonds may have reached a top already and could well underperform, possibly quite sharply, in 1998," he added.

Porzecanski said Brazil's so-called soveriegn risk was sharply reduced in recent years due to a series of positive factors, beginning with the success of the government's three-year-old anti-inflation and stabilization Real Plan.

"It has allowed for a sense of sanity to pervade Brazilian society for the first time in decades and for hope to be born again," he said. But economic reforms in Brazil are moving much too slowly and appear to be getting diluted, he added.
"I remember writing not too long ago...that gradualist Brazil was a tortoise and not a hare in the racetrack of modernization," he said.
"I have to admit, I do wonder whether the tortoise has fallen asleep and is ever going to make it to the finish line."

Porzecanski also said constitutional reforms lack enabling legislation or regulatory watchdogs and the government has not given deregulation a high enough priority, making it unable to overcome strong lobbies favoring the status quo.
"The bloated public sector remains largely unreformed ... And reform of the unfunded social security system is also stuck in Congress," he wrote.

He also said he was concerned that Brazil's three-year-old currency, the real, was overvalued. Of particular concern, according to Porzecanski, is currency risk in 1998. He noted that Brazil's borrowing requirements are much larger than its current account gap suggests.
"As long as world liquidity remains ample and there is confidence in Brazil, there should be no problem filling this potential gap," he said.

But Porzecanski praised President Fernando Henrique Cardoso as a man with a global vision and common sense who has improved Brazil's notoriously skewed income distribution, revamped its foreign relations and regained its old position as hub of foreign investment in South America.

"The Brazilian people are so grateful to him for having slain the dragon of hyperinflation that they have made him the most popular president in the Americas," he added. "He will probably run for re-election and be re-elected easily in 1998."
